h: The Sangh joins the fight: asking about your vote will now be called a 'conspiracy'
dek: Senior journalist Anand K. Sahay argues that after Mohan Bhagwat's Vijayadashami speech, the RSS has openly taken the field against the anti-SIR movement, and the government and the Sangh are speaking in one voice.
body: According to senior journalist Anand K. Sahay, Mohan Bhagwat's Vijayadashami speech was a clear signal: the Sangh is now ready to take on directly the movement in which young people, citizens' groups and opposition parties together accuse the Election Commission of tampering with voters through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). The writer fears the crackdown will grow.

He alleges that Hindutva activists entered the protests and, along with the police, raised their hands against protesters. In his 20 October speech, Bhagwat called these protests, without any evidence, a conspiracy hatched at foreign bidding, and compared them with Europe and Bangladesh.

In the same period, Prime Minister Modi took aim at Rahul Gandhi and his family at a media event in Delhi and blamed the Congress for the unrest among the young. The same day Amit Shah struck up the old 'infiltrators' tune that has played through many elections. The writer reminds us that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar himself has avoided saying how many infiltrators the revision found.

Sahay's sharpest point is that Modi and Bhagwat both paint critics as people out to destabilise the country, but neither has answered the charge at the heart of the movement: more than 13 crore names cut from the voter rolls. The question was about an account; the answer came in the language of patriotism and conspiracy.

The writer sees the Sangh's claim to be a 'cultural organisation' as an ideological veil. He recalls the charges Sardar Patel made after Gandhi's murder, and mentions protest photographs by Raihan Vadra being removed from an exhibition in Delhi. In his view the Sangh has now formally entered this fight, and the country stands at a turning point.
nazar: When a question raised about a constitutional body is answered with words like 'foreign hand' and 'infiltrator', the debate moves from accounts to loyalty. The heaviest price is paid by those whose names are cut first: Muslims, Dalits, Adivasis, migrant workers and women, who are first pushed off the list and then put under suspicion.

An unelected organisation openly stepping in against a street movement is a warning for democracy. Before the 1 November rally, the real question is the one that keeps being dodged: if names were cut, why, and whose?
sawal: Is someone who asks for an account of their own name a conspirator?
ref: Vijayadashami speech
Every year on Dussehra the RSS chief gives a speech from Nagpur. The Sangh was founded on this day in 1925, so the speech is seen as the organisation's direction for the year.
SIR (Special Intensive Revision)
A fresh check of the voter rolls in which links to old rolls or documents are demanded. The opposition alleges it has cut the names of eligible people on a large scale.
ank: Alleged: names cut from voter rolls
Years since the Sangh was founded on Vijayadashami

h: From ration to vote: the same old recipe of weeding out
dek: Sociologist Veena Naregal says the SIR method is not new. It is the 'freeze and filter' model tried for ten years on rations, health care and MGNREGA, now applied to the right to vote.
body: Veena Naregal, professor of sociology at Delhi's Institute of Economic Growth, says those surprised by the SIR forget that this method has already been tried on welfare schemes. The only difference is that this time the right to vote is at stake.

She recalls that from the 1993 voter cards to the photo rolls of 2009, India's rolls had become fairly clean; former Chief Election Commissioner S.Y. Quraishi considered them about 99 per cent accurate. The SIR made the 2024 roll meaningless: only those on a roll about two decades old were treated as eligible, and the rest had to show a link to parents or grandparents, or papers. By 1 September, 13.37 crore names were missing from the draft rolls.

Then the writer turns to the period after 2015. Ration list numbers were frozen at the 2011 population, and orders came to match them with voter rolls and report cuts every quarter. By the estimate of Jean Drèze and Reetika Khera, about 10 crore people were left out of rations by 2020. In Andhra and Telangana lists were pruned by matching with Aadhaar, where researcher Srinivas Kodali alleged that 46 lakh names were cut.

Naregal calls this the 'freeze and filter' model. In the SIR too, unpublished software rules flag voters for 'logical discrepancy' and as 'unmapped'. From July 2026 the online Form 6 added a question that is not in the legal form at all, and two election commissioners objected. In Bengal, judges hearing appeals found that the system cannot add back a cut name even on a court's order.

Her conclusion is that those who celebrated the 2018 Aadhaar judgment as a victory for privacy did not see the people being pushed out of the ration queue. Now the same machinery has reached every voter's door.
nazar: This article takes the SIR out of being a one-off event and places it in a long chain. The poor families who were first denied grain because of thumbprints, server failures and missing papers are now at the greatest risk of being dropped from the roll: Dalits, Adivasis, migrant workers, and women whose papers lie scattered between their parents' home and their in-laws'.

The lesson is clear: as long as there was silence on cuts in welfare schemes, this tool kept getting sharper. If the right to vote is to be saved, the right to food and work is part of the same fight.
sawal: First the name went from the plate, now from the roll. What next?
ref: Puttaswamy judgment
In 2017 a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court held privacy to be a fundamental right. Even so, the 2018 Aadhaar judgment let Aadhaar stay mandatory for welfare schemes.
Form 6
The legal form for enrolling as a new voter. The dispute is that old voters cut in the SIR are also being made to fill it.

h: Democracy of batons and guns: a sign of panic, not strength
dek: Jamia student Sharmeen Shah argues that sending paramilitary forces against peaceful protests, from anti-SIR students to Manipur and Arunachal, shows the government's weakness.
body: Sharmeen Shah, a student at Jamia Millia Islamia, writes that India now goes beyond the police and turns to paramilitary forces to deal with dissent. In her view a government that lines up guns even in front of a peaceful crowd shows not its strength but its panic.

The writer begins with the student protests in Delhi against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter rolls and demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. According to the article, forces were flown in from border areas, and the Home Ministry, citing fears of sudden protests, extended the deployment of six forces including the CRPF, BSF and ITBP until 31 October. At Jamia the ITBP was posted near students on hunger strike for a students' union, while the same force is handling tension on the China border.

The writer says this is not limited to Delhi. In East Siang in Arunachal, tear gas and batons were used against protests over the Siang dam, and in Manipur on 23 October tear gas was fired at a protest where people banged pots and pans. At Chaityabhoomi in Mumbai, 20 to 25 people were detained from a candlelight gathering in memory of IIT Bombay student Sahil Wakode. Caste harassment is alleged behind Sahil's death.

The article cites ACLED data showing that by 2 October there were about 19,500 protests in the country and the police intervened in at least 1,200. In the Global Peace Index 2026, India slipped from 115th to 127th among 163 countries. The UN human rights office raised concern about arbitrary detention, which the government called unwanted interference.

Sharmeen Shah concludes that this growing use of force on students and peaceful gatherings is a sign of the decline of democratic conduct, and that a government that sees every voice as a threat is frightened inside.
nazar: When forces built to guard the border stand at university gates, the question is not only of law and order but of the relationship between citizen and state. The heaviest price falls on those whose voices are already weak: Muslim and Dalit students, the Adivasis of Manipur and Arunachal, farmers to be uprooted by a dam.
Questions about the right to vote should be answered with dialogue and openness, not with the barrel of a gun.
sawal: Why are border troops standing in front of peaceful students?
ref: ACLED
An independent body that gathers data on protests and political violence around the world. Its data is widely used in research and the media.
Global Peace Index
An annual ranking by the Institute for Economics and Peace that measures countries on internal violence, militarisation and conflict.

h: Jantar Mantar from London to Sydney: the Indian diaspora breaks its silence
dek: Writing in Qaumi Awaz, Uppsala University professor Ashok Swain says protests among Indians abroad under the name 'Jantar Mantar is everywhere' are shaking the base of Modi's image overseas, though this awakening is still incomplete.
body: Ashok Swain recalls that the real strength of the Prime Minister's foreign tours has been less diplomacy and more the diaspora crowds prepared by embassies. Pictures of these 'Modi, Modi' rallies sold the story at home that Indians all over the world stood behind one leader. Now cracks are showing on that same stage.

According to the writer, students, professionals and workers in cities such as London, New York, Toronto, Sydney, Berlin, Dublin, Stockholm, Copenhagen and The Hague have gathered under the banner 'Jantar Mantar is everywhere'. They demand an account of the alleged election irregularities, free and fair elections, and an end to the repression of protesters.

He warns against haste. The diaspora is divided by religion, caste, class and race, and in the 2024 Carnegie survey 47 per cent of people of Indian origin in America were satisfied with Modi's work. Still, Sikh groups since the farmers' movement, and anti-caste, Muslim and student groups from even earlier, have challenged Hindutva politics. What is new is that people who stayed away from politics until now have also started speaking after seeing police harshness against peaceful protesters.

The cost of fear is also real. The writer mentions actor Imran Khan, an OCI cardholder who, according to reports, was told to leave the country after joining a protest in Mumbai. He has gone to court, but the message for others is clear: speaking out could close the road home.

Swain believes Western governments will act according to arms, trade and China, so expectations from them should be low. The real work of the diaspora is to explain in universities, the media and civil society that criticising Modi is not opposing India, and that electoral freedom and minority rights are India's own questions.
nazar: For years rallies like Madison Square Garden were presented at home as proof that those questioning the government were a handful. Now that the same diaspora cities are sending back the echo of Jantar Mantar, it is a measure of the movement's moral reach.
But the Imran Khan case is a warning. Turning the OCI card into a tool of punishment frightens lakhs of families whose roots are here, and Muslim, Sikh and Dalit emigrants are the first targets.
sawal: Will voices raised abroad give strength to the street here?
ref: OCI card
Overseas Citizenship of India: a status given to people of Indian origin with foreign citizenship, which lets them travel to India without a visa. The government can also cancel it.
Indian American Attitudes Survey
A Carnegie Endowment survey that measures the political views of people of Indian origin living in America.

h: By Gandhi's test: the right to vote is also a satyagraha
dek: S.N. Sahoo argues that cutting a name from the voter roll takes away the citizen's most basic tool for putting direct pressure on power, and that is why the movement staying non-violent gives hope.
body: S.N. Sahoo begins with the Prime Minister's 13 October speech in which India was called the 'mother of democracy'. According to the writer, at that very time heavy deployments and internet shutdowns in Delhi were holding back students who were demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. He claims that about 20 crore people were dropped from the rolls by the SIR in 21 states, and the Prime Minister is silent on it.

Then he turns to Gandhi. In 1931, in a committee of the Round Table Conference, Gandhi said that in 1896 in Durban his name had been put on the roll without his knowledge, because someone wanted his vote. The same year, in Young India, he called adult franchise direct action, and satyagraha stronger than that. Sahoo argues that cutting a name snatches exactly this direct action from the citizen's hands.

The writer lists the course of the movement: protests from 2 October, the opposition's march on 10 October, a 'people's impeachment' at Kharge's house when police did not allow the Ashok Hotel, and the 'Save the vote, save the country' rally at Ramlila Maidan on 1 November. He points out that on 28 October there were no barricades on the route of the BJP president's march in Chandni Chowk.

In the Supreme Court, the bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant asked why people who were already on the roll were being made to fill Form 6. Sahoo recalls the standing the Commission once earned in the time of the first Chief Election Commissioner, Sukumar Sen.

Finally he stresses that despite mass detentions the movement has stayed non-violent, and that Neha Bora of AISA refused to sign a peace bond. Citing research, he holds that non-violent protest strengthens its cause, and that this is a good sign for democracy.
nazar: The weight of Sahoo's argument lies in seeing the vote not as a ritual but as power. For the worker, farmer or Dalit woman who has neither money nor influence, the vote is the one tool with which she asks power for an account. Cutting her name is silencing her.

The double standard on barricades is no small thing either: when one side's march passes along an open road and the city is shut for the other, questions about equality before the law will arise. The movement's non-violence is its greatest asset, and keeping it intact is its own responsibility.
sawal: When someone's vote is taken away, what is left to them but satyagraha?
ref: Round Table Conference (1930-32)
Meetings in London between the British government and Indian leaders on India's constitutional future. Gandhi was the Congress's only representative at the second conference in 1931.
Sukumar Sen
India's first Chief Election Commissioner, who held the first general election of 1951-52. With crores of first-time voters, it was the world's biggest electoral experiment.

h: On paper ballots the BJP lost Kashi: the message of the MLC results
dek: In Navjivan, Nagendra writes that on Uttar Pradesh's graduate and teacher seats, where votes were cast on paper ballots, the BJP's defeats in Varanasi and Lucknow have sharpened both the anger of educated voters and the EVM versus ballot debate.
body: Of the 11 graduate and teacher seats in the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council, the BJP won 6 and the Samajwadi Party 5, so the tally stayed as before. But according to Nagendra the real story is in the map: both seats of Varanasi, the Prime Minister's own constituency, went to the SP, the Lucknow graduate seat slipped from the BJP's hands, and there was a jolt in Agra too.

The writer says that in religious cities such as Kashi, the Agra division that includes Mathura, and Prayagraj, teachers and graduates put jobs, paper leaks, the old pension and rising prices first. It looks like the next link after the 2024 defeat in Ayodhya. Chief Minister Yogi campaigned with the whole administrative machinery, and still the BJP candidate in Gorakhpur won by only 307 votes.

One important point is that all these elections were held on paper ballots. According to the writer, defeat on the ballot in big cities has put the ruling side on the defensive and given the opposition, which has been questioning EVMs, a psychological argument, though the BJP won Meerut and Gorakhpur.

Quoting Yogesh, who writes on youth politics, the article calls this a ground survey of 72 districts, with one to one and a half lakh votes cast on each seat. The Madhyamik Shikshak Sangh, which dominated teacher seats for decades, has no representative left for the first time in nearly fifty years.

Nagendra believes this does not prove that Yogi's administrative grip has weakened, but the anger of the urban educated class with the double engine government is plain to see, and before 2027 it is a warning bell for the BJP.
nazar: This article does not name the movement, but it tests one of its demands on the ground. At the very time the INDIA alliance is challenging the government to dissolve Parliament and hold elections by ballot, paper ballots showed a different picture in the Prime Minister's stronghold. It would be wrong to treat this as proof of any rigging, but it does give strength to the debate about trust.

Questions like paper leaks and the old pension belong to the same generation that is sitting at Jantar Mantar. The anger of teachers and jobless graduates is not separate from the fight over voter rolls; both demand accountability.
sawal: Will the paper ballot resolve the crisis of trust?
ref: Graduate and teacher constituencies
Legislative Council seats where only registered graduates or teachers vote. Voting here is by preference on ballot papers, not on EVMs.
PDA
The Samajwadi Party's slogan: Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak (backward classes, Dalits, minorities), on which it builds its social coalition.

h: A dissenting voice on the language of 'regime change'
dek: Kaushlesh Rai, founder of The Dossier, believes that about 70 lakh names wrongly cut in the SIR is a real problem that can be fixed, but says the movement's leaders are turning it into a fight to change the government.
body: This article is a measured voice against the movement, and that is why it is worth reading. Kaushlesh Rai begins with Prashant Bhushan's remark at the Press Club on 15 October that everyone wants a change of government, while the printed demands were limited to the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation, release of those detained, an end to police action and reopening Jantar Mantar.

Then he unpacks the '13 crore' figure. According to him, in the check of 95.40 crore names, 13.39 crore were flagged at the draft stage: 6.30 crore had moved elsewhere, 3.01 crore were absent, 2.80 crore were dead and 1.02 crore were duplicates. The Commission does not treat this as the final cut. Rai also accepts that in the previous eight intensive revisions the rolls grew, and this is the first in which they shrank.

Relying on Surjit Bhalla's estimate, he says that in states where the roll has been finalised, about 70 lakh eligible voters were removed without proper reason, and in appeals most were found eligible, so their names should come back. But his assessment is that seven out of eight names were cut for the right reason.

The writer lists past allegations, from EVMs to Mahadevapura and Haryana, and in his view none of them held up. He also recalls that in the Navin Chawla case, the Congress itself did not give much weight to the question of the Commission's fairness.

His last argument is about words: this language of changing the government usually points to a path outside elections, and praise for the Bangladesh movement adds to this suspicion. According to the writer, the real issue is the 70 lakh names, which must be put right.
nazar: We are carrying this article because the movement should also face the strongest argument against it. But note this: even a critic accepts that about 70 lakh eligible people were dropped from the roll without reason. That figure on its own is a shame for any democracy, and the poor, migrant workers and marginalised communities are likely to make up a large share of them.
Words can be argued over, but changing a government through elections is a normal part of democracy, not a conspiracy. The real question is that the election be held on a clean and complete roll.
sawal: Are seventy lakh cut names a small slip or a great injustice?
ref: Navin Chawla controversy

In 2009 the then Chief Election Commissioner N. Gopalaswami recommended removing Commissioner Navin Chawla over charges of bias. The government did not accept it, and Chawla later became Chief Election Commissioner himself.
Form 17C
The record of votes cast at a polling station, given to candidates' agents. The Commission cites it in disputes over voting figures.

h: My blind-follower friend is back. What do I do with him now?
dek: Using the return of an old friend, senior journalist Krishna Pratap Singh asks how democracy should treat the disillusioned devotees of the hero worship that the youth upsurge has shattered.
body: The article opens with a personal story. Until four or five years ago a friend came by almost every other day and flared up at the slightest disagreement. At their last meeting the writer quoted Ambedkar: devotion in religion may lead to salvation, but in politics it brings democracy down. The friend called him a traitor and left. Now he has come back with folded hands, saying he is no longer a bhakt (devotee).

According to Krishna Pratap Singh, the fault is not one person's. In 76 years of the Constitution, citizens could not keep away from hero worship. The disease was there in Indira's time too, but then institutions that held it back were still alive to some extent. After 2014, in the writer's words, a 'development man' who came riding on big capital mixed religion, politics and promises to create such a divide of us and them that the institutions meant to stop it became nearly lifeless.

The writer describes how bhakts behave: refusing reason and data, getting more aggressive when cornered, branding critics anti-national. He also sets out the scholars' debate that not every blind follower is a fascist, but the two share things like avoiding reason, demanding total loyalty and hating dissent.

Then, the writer says, the Gen Z upsurge came like a storm, and the bhakts found no place in it. Their claims were exposed and they began to hide their faces. The friend who returned also admits that he had mistaken a jackal for a lion.

But as he leaves, the friend drops a stinging question: if the writer turns him away, how democratic will the writer himself remain? The writer admits he has no answer, and asks readers to think about it too.
nazar: This is where the movement's real test lies. If the young people on the streets only replace one hero with another, Ambedkar's warning will go unheard again. Giving returning bhakts a place in debate instead of taunts is hard, but democracy is built from exactly this hardship.
We must also remember that Muslims, Dalits and dissenting voices paid the biggest price for hero worship. The road to forgiveness goes through acknowledging their pain, not forgetting it.
sawal: Embrace the disillusioned bhakt, or ask for accountability?
ref: Ambedkar's speech of 25 November 1949
His last speech in the Constituent Assembly, in which he warned that bhakti or hero worship in politics is a road to dictatorship.
Gen Z
The generation born between 1997 and 2012. A large number of the students and young people in this movement come from it.

h: The fourth pillar is not the newspaper owner but the citizen who speaks
dek: Anil Chamadia argues that the Constitution gives freedom of expression to the people, and media companies have written this right in their own name.
body: We often assume that after the legislature, judiciary and executive, the media is democracy's fourth pillar. Senior journalist Anil Chamadia questions this common belief. According to him, the Constitution mentions no fourth pillar, and the balance imagined between the three organs has not been achieved either. On top of that, the writer says, the media has formed an unholy alliance with power.

The article recalls that calling the press the fourth estate goes back to Edmund Burke, while for thinkers like Locke and Voltaire the real point was a human being's freedom to speak. In India, Article 19(1)(a) gives this freedom to the people. There is no separate mention of freedom of the press or media. That means newspapers and channels are only a means of expression, not its owners.

By Chamadia's reckoning, the media deserves to be called a pillar only when it helps citizens keep watch on the three organs of power, expose their failings, demand accountability and protect basic rights. But most media houses are private companies with their own economic, social and political interests. Should these interests also be treated as part of democracy?

Giving a historical example, the writer says that under British rule the newspapers of big companies were not at the front of the freedom struggle; ordinary people organised the fight. After independence, many MPs complained in Parliament that newspaper owners suppressed the people's voice for their own profit. In the August 1955 debate on the first Press Commission's report, too, the race to capture the press is visible.

The writer claims that today the country's media is in the hands of about 50 companies, and the citizen's expression has been 'outsourced' to them. If a group of citizens keeps watch, it will look to the public interest; if a company does, it will look to its own profit and loss. So the real fourth pillar is the people themselves.
nazar: This argument matters for those whose voices never find room in big media: Dalits, Adivasis, minorities, workers and farmers. When newsrooms shrink into the hands of a few companies and a few castes, 'freedom of the press' often becomes the owner's freedom.

The way to save democracy is not just better channels but protecting citizens' own platforms, community media and spaces to speak. If the fourth pillar is the people, every curb on their tongue is a blow to democracy.
sawal: Whose is the freedom of the press, the owner's or the reader's?
ref: Article 19(1)(a)
The provision of the Constitution that gives every citizen freedom of speech and expression. Press freedom has been drawn from it; it is not written separately.
First Press Commission
A commission set up in 1952 that reported on newspaper ownership, monopolies and the condition of journalists. Parliament debated it in 1955.

h: America's 'transshipment scam': heavy charges, light evidence
dek: Former customs chief Najib Shah says there is no solid data behind the list on which the White House has put India at the top.
body: In August 2026 the White House released a document alleging that exporters linked to China are dodging US tariffs by sending goods through 40 countries. The list puts India in 'Tier 1', meaning the highest risk. Najib Shah, former chairman of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes, examines the document and finds it weak.

The writer first explains that transshipment is not theft but an everyday part of sea trade. More than 80 per cent of the world's goods travel by sea, and big ships do not stop at every port, so goods change ships at ports along the way. Singapore, Colombo and Jebel Ali are such hubs, and India is working to make Vizhinjam in Kerala one too.

According to Shah, the document's only evidence is that imports from China fell and imports from other countries rose. It estimates losses of 40 to 303 billion dollars, but the claim of 67 billion dollars of goods routed through India, Mexico and Vietnam is not even split among the three. Its list of pumps includes Pune and Gujarat, but leaves out Coimbatore, the country's big pump hub.

The writer also points out that the aim of cutting imports through tariffs has itself failed: US imports grew from 2.41 trillion dollars in 2017 to 3.50 trillion in 2025. If real value is added to goods or their classification changes, then under the rules they are that country's goods. Action should be taken against the American importer who makes a false declaration, not against the country in between.

Shah does not defend China; he only asks for evidence. The WTO's Bali agreement recognises transshipment, and India's 2020 CAROTAR rules show how the origin of goods can be checked without defaming any country.
nazar: This debate is not only about ships and papers. The livelihoods of lakhs of workers in pump factories and small export units in Coimbatore, Pune or Gujarat depend on whether a stamp of suspicion is put on their goods. A tariff imposed on a baseless charge first eats up small businesses and the jobs of contract workers.

The lesson for the Indian government is that staying quiet under pressure from a country it calls a 'friend' costs dearly. Asking for evidence is a question of sovereignty, not hostility towards anyone.
sawal: Who finally carries the burden of a baseless tariff?
ref: Transshipment
Unloading goods from one ship at a port along the way and sending them on in another. In itself this is a legal and common trade practice.
Rules of origin
The rules that decide which country a product is considered to come from. If enough value is added to goods in a country, or their form changes, they are counted as that country's.

h: The graves of Chemmani: half-done probes will not bring justice
dek: A report on more than 580 skeletons found near Jaffna has reopened old wounds, and Jehan Perera asks when Sri Lanka will build a credible system for reaching the truth.
body: After months of digging at Chemmani near Jaffna in northern Sri Lanka, more than 580 skeletons have been found. The final report of forensic archaeologist Professor Raj Somadeva says the site looks more like a regular cemetery than a place where bodies were secretly buried, but also accepts that the evidence is not enough to settle the circumstances of burial. This conclusion, unlike the two earlier interim reports, has unsettled the families of the missing.

Jehan Perera recalls that this has happened before. In 2013, 154 skeletons were dug up from a hospital compound in Matale, and experts clashed over their age. In 2018 a laboratory in America dated some samples from the Mannar grave to about 600 years ago, even though a biscuit wrapper from the 1980s and a skeleton in handcuffs had been found there. Passing judgment on a whole site from a few samples, the writer says, is dangerous.

Chemmani's name has been tied to this since 1996. A soldier convicted of the rape and murder of schoolgirl Krishanthi Kumaraswamy claimed that hundreds of arrested Tamil civilians had been killed and buried there. More than 15,000 cases of people who went missing during the war are on record.

The writer also lists the gaps in the new report. It names no epidemic and no disaster, gives no date or cause of death, and does not rule out unlawful killings. School bags have been found with some of the remains, and families have challenged the report in court.

He sees the way forward in the Human Rights Commission's recommendations: international experts for dating and DNA tests, a DNA bank for relatives, a fixed method for excavation, and an independent body to prosecute officers for serious crimes. In his view, talk of reconciliation is hollow without telling families what happened to their loved ones.
nazar: The question of mass graves is not Sri Lanka's alone. Demands for a probe into the unmarked graves of Kashmir have been pending for years, and families of people who vanished in custody or in 'encounters' have been seeking answers in many states. When the probe is in the hands of the very system that stands accused, even science starts speaking the language of power.

The DNA bank and independent investigating body Perera suggests are a useful model for us too. The trust of minority and Adivasi families will return only when they themselves take part in the search for the truth.
sawal: How long must those whose loved ones are missing keep waiting?
ref: Chemmani
An area near Jaffna in northern Sri Lanka. There have long been allegations that Tamil civilians made to disappear in the 1990s were buried here.
Office on Missing Persons
A Sri Lankan government office set up under a 2016 law, which keeps records of and searches for people who went missing during the civil war.

h: Mada Masr shut down: a dark day for free journalism in Egypt
dek: A Cairo court has ordered an independent news site closed and a heavy fine on its editor, and journalist Sharif Abdel Kouddous, who once worked there, explains why the verdict came now.
by: Sharif Abdel Kouddous (in conversation with Amy Goodman and Nermeen Shaikh)
body: On 27 October a Cairo court ordered Egypt's independent news website Mada Masr shut down, its assets seized, and its editor Lina Attalah fined 3 million Egyptian pounds, about 50,000 dollars. The offence named was running a website without a licence, and Lina was ordered held until the fine was paid. According to a later report, she was released on 28 October.

Sharif Abdel Kouddous, Middle East editor of Drop Site News, who spent four years at Mada Masr, called it a dark day for journalism across the Arab world. Started in 2013 amid the upheaval of revolution and counter-revolution, the site has faced arrests, deportation of foreign staff, raids on its office and about ten years of blocking.

According to Kouddous, the hearing was a mere formality. The defence got no chance to see the file, others were cleared from the court and plainclothes security men seated instead, every request to present witnesses and documents was rejected, and the judge appointed a lawyer for Lina himself despite objections. Then the harshest sentence was handed down and security men carried her out.

Why now? Kouddous says that a month earlier the whole newsroom of the fact-checking group Matsadaqsh, six journalists, was arrested, and he alleges they were beaten into recording false confessions. President Sisi has spoken of stepping down when his term ends, but Kouddous does not see this as a democratic change.

His big worry is that the world's attention is on elections in Brazil, Serbia and Israel, the US midterms and Gaza, and in this noise Egypt could quietly finish off an institution. Earlier, foreign pressure and solidarity at home saved Lina and her colleagues. This time too, loud voices from journalists and from America are needed; Egypt is the second-largest recipient of US aid.
nazar: In India too, laws on licences, registration and foreign funding have been seen becoming tools to corner free media and citizens' groups. The Mada Masr case shows that censorship no longer needs an outright ban; a paperwork offence and a heavy fine are enough.
Small, independent and often women-led outlets are the ones that bring the news power wants to hide. They will be protected only by solidarity across borders.
sawal: When the court itself puts on the lock, where will the news go?
ref: Mada Masr
An Egyptian news site started in 2013 by Lina Attalah and colleagues, known for investigative reporting in Arabic and English. It has been blocked in Egypt since 2017.
Drop Site News
An independent American investigative news outlet started in 2024, reporting on war, foreign policy and the Middle East.

h: Loan conditions, workers' pockets: unions take on the IMF
dek: Two labour leaders from Thailand and the Asia-Pacific explain why workers and ordinary consumers end up paying the bill for cuts, privatisation and the debt burden.
body: On 16 October more than a thousand workers marched in Bangkok against the IMF and the World Bank. It was part of a global day of protest in more than 150 cities in 38 countries. Thai labour leader Sawit Kaewvarn and Kate Lappin of Public Services International complain that the media showed the clashes, not what the workers had to say.

Their figures make the debt picture clear. Developing countries are paying on average 9.5 per cent of their government revenue just in interest, the highest in 25 years and more than three times that of rich countries. A record 61 countries spend at least a tenth of their revenue on interest, and in 2024 developing countries paid 384 billion dollars in interest on external debt.

The writers argue that the conditions that come with loans push governments towards cutting spending, taxes that fall heavily on ordinary people, and caps on public sector wages. The result is hiring freezes, staff shortages in schools and hospitals, and the unpaid burden of care on women's shoulders. The worker pays twice, once from their wages and again through weaker public services.

Pakistan is their sharpest example. According to the writers, the IMF wants the full sale of what is left of the public power system, while over the past two years more than 60 per cent of payments to power companies were capacity payments, that is, money for electricity that was never produced. In Thailand after the 1997 crisis, unions stopped the full privatisation of the Electricity Generating Authority, but airports and telecom were partly sold off.

As alternatives they demand curbs on corporate profits, a global wealth tax on billionaires, and an end to predatory debt structures and conditions. This is a partisan article by union leaders, and many claims are their own assessments.
nazar: India does not run on IMF loans, but the recipe of disinvestment, contract hiring in government jobs and privatising power distribution is the same here. The protests of electricity employees from Uttar Pradesh to Chandigarh are part of this debate.

When staff shrink in government schools and hospitals, Dalit, Adivasi and poor women are hit first. This experience from the neighbourhood reminds us that any 'reform' should be counted against the pockets of workers and consumers.
sawal: Who pays the bill for electricity that was never produced?
ref: Capacity payment
A fixed amount in power purchase agreements that the government pays private power plants for staying ready, whether or not power is bought from them.
Public Services International
A global federation of public service workers' unions, with unions from more than 150 countries.

h: Barring women from jobs in toddy shops is unconstitutional: High Court
dek: A widow was refused her husband's job; the High Court struck down the very rule that kept women out of toddy shops.
body: On Thursday the Kerala High Court struck down the rule that barred women from any work in toddy (palm wine) shops. Justice P. Gopinath held Rule 7(37) of the Kerala Abkari Shops Disposal Rules, 2002 to be against equality, protection from discrimination, freedom of employment and the right to life.

The case is that of Sophy from Thrissur district. Her husband worked at a toddy shop, and after his death Sophy asked for a job there on compassionate grounds. She was refused, citing this rule. Her lawyers pointed out that courts have already removed similar bans in foreign liquor shops, and that these rulings rest on the Supreme Court's Anuj Garg case.

The state government argued that toddy shops are often in lonely places, so the rule was meant to protect women from exploitation and harassment. The government also said the liquor trade is a business in which no claim of fundamental right arises. The shop's licensee also sided with the government, saying that the sale of loose toddy carries more risk.

The court did not accept these arguments. The core of the verdict is that providing a safe workplace is the government's duty, and this duty cannot be met by shutting women out of an entire trade. No solid basis for danger at toddy shops was placed on record either. The court said Sophy's application should be reconsidered setting this rule aside, and no such licence condition would stand either.
nazar: Keeping women out of work in the name of protection is an old method, and it hits hardest the women of poor homes for whom a compassionate appointment is the only support. The Kerala High Court rightly said that if there is danger, improve the arrangements; do not shut the door. This test should apply to similar rules in other states too.
sawal: What kind of justice takes away a woman's livelihood to protect her?
ref: Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association (2007)
A Supreme Court ruling that struck down a ban on women working in places that serve liquor. The court said equality cannot be taken away in the name of protection.
Compassionate appointment
A job given to the dependant of an employee who dies, so that the family is not suddenly left without support.

h: Citing the Vedas and Manusmriti, court gives three Muslims life terms
dek: A Gandhinagar sessions court wrote the opening pages of its verdict in a cow slaughter case on religious texts, while in Damoh, Madhya Pradesh, buffalo traders were beaten and a case was filed against them too.
body: On Monday a sessions court in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, sentenced three Muslim men, Wasim Qureshi, Mohammad Rafiq Qureshi and Ashfaq Bahelim, to life in prison in a cow slaughter case. Each was also fined three lakh rupees. They were convicted under several sections, including the Gujarat Animal Preservation (Amendment) Act and the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act.

According to the report, the first four pages of the verdict are about the importance of the cow in Hinduism. They cite the Vedas and the Manusmriti and record the belief that 33 crore gods live in the cow. The court wrote that the accused knew the cow is regarded as a mother and still slaughtered it cruelly, and that if such people are not punished, the cow could disappear.

According to the prosecution, the men bought old or dry cattle cheaply and slaughtered them for trade. Police claimed to have seized about 277 kg of beef when it was being readied for sale. The report does not name the judge who gave the verdict.

The same report also records an incident from Damoh in Madhya Pradesh. It is alleged that people linked to a Hindutva group accused two Muslim traders carrying buffaloes, and the van driver, of theft, tied them up, dragged them through a field and beat them with sticks. Police registered a case against unknown attackers, but also filed a case against the victims for cramming buffaloes into a small van.
nazar: A court's job is to weigh law and evidence, not to make one religion's faith the basis of its verdict. When a court that runs on the Constitution cites the Manusmriti to hand down life sentences, it is not only the Muslim accused who are troubled, but Dalits and every citizen that text did not treat as equal. The Damoh incident shows how the same thinking emboldens mobs on the street and police in the station. This verdict must be tested in a higher court.
sawal: What place does the Manusmriti have in a court of the Constitution?
ref: Gujarat Animal Preservation (Amendment) Act, 2017
An amendment in Gujarat that provides for up to life imprisonment for cow slaughter, counted among the country's strictest cattle laws.
Manusmriti
An ancient law text with discriminatory rules about caste and women. Ambedkar publicly burned it in 1927.

h: Panskura: mob attacks Adivasi Christian family, Bibles thrown into a pond
dek: Parvati Hembram Soren, 27, of Purba Medinipur alleges that a mob of thirty beat her for an hour and pressured her to give up her faith. An FIR has been filed but no one has been arrested.
body: An attack on a Christian family has been alleged on the evening of 26 October in Paschim Arjunda village in the Panskura area of Purba Medinipur district, West Bengal. According to 27-year-old Parvati Hembram Soren, a mob of about thirty people reached the house at 7.30 in the evening. It included distant relatives of her family, neighbours and people linked to the Vishva Hindu Parishad.

Parvati alleges that the mob snatched and threw away Bibles, tried to burn them and dumped four copies into a nearby pond. She was slapped, kicked and punched, dragged by her hair and her clothes were torn. All this went on for about an hour and she fainted. Her sister-in-law was also beaten, and her phone was snatched and videos deleted from it. The family became Christian a year ago, and according to Parvati the attackers were threatening to kill them and cast them out unless they returned to Hinduism.

This was not the first incident. On 11 October too, people calling themselves Bajrang Dal members had come to the house. A complaint was sent by email the next day, but the police did nothing. When the police were called during the attack, the reply was that the attackers would call the police themselves. Later the family was told to pray inside the house and not to use a speaker.

On 28 October an FIR was filed under sections for hurt, theft, house trespass, threats and assault with intent to disrobe a woman, naming about ten relatives. No arrest had been made at the time of reporting. The district SP and Additional SP did not answer their phones.
nazar: Parvati is Adivasi, a woman and a Christian, and she paid the price for all three identities in a single evening. This series of attacks on Christian families in Bengal can no longer be called isolated incidents. The most dangerous thing is the police's attitude, asking the victim herself to hide her worship. Article 25 of the Constitution gives every citizen the right to follow their religion, and protecting it is the police's job.
sawal: Since when has praying in your own home become a crime?
ref: Article 25
The provision of the Constitution that gives every person the freedom to profess, practise and propagate their religion.
Bangiya Khristiya Pariseva
An organisation of Bengal's Christians whose legal team is helping victims of the recent attacks.

h: Race Course mosque: it won't be demolished, but no permission to pray either
dek: The Delhi High Court said that because of security concerns it cannot force the government to open the 150-year-old mosque near the Prime Minister's residence.
body: A plea to let worshippers into Delhi's Race Course mosque got no relief from the Delhi High Court on Thursday. Justice Anish Dayal said demolition is going on nearby and there is a question of security, so the court cannot order the government to open the mosque. The petition was filed by Syed Ahmed Saud, who prays there and calls it a matter of religious freedom under Article 25.

According to the petition, the mosque near the Prime Minister's residence is more than 150 years old, was notified as waqf property in 1977, and got Grade-II heritage status in a 2009 Delhi government notification. On 7 October, while nearby slums were being cleared, the mosque's electricity and water were cut, even though it was not on the list of encroachments. On 17 October an official of the Land and Development Office arrived with police and it was said that the mosque would be demolished in two to four days.

The Centre's lawyer Ashish Dixit told the court that the mosque would not be demolished until the Delhi Waqf Board decides on the plea to save it. But going there cannot be allowed amid the demolition, and no one is being allowed into a temple in the area either. The court accepted this statement and asked who would pay compensation if someone were hurt.

The petitioner's lawyer M. Sufian Siddiqui showed photographs and said there is nothing left around to demolish, so the way in and out should be opened. The court recorded both sides' statements and asked the government for a status report.
nazar: The assurance that the mosque will not be torn down rests not on a court order but on the government's own statement, and the country has seen many times recently how fragile such assurances are. Stopping worship in the name of security even after the rubble around it has been cleared raises questions. The argument of equal restrictions on the temple does not hide the fact that it was the mosque's power and water that were cut first.
sawal: Where nothing is left to demolish, security from whom?
ref: Waqf property
Property dedicated permanently by Muslims for religious or charitable purposes, looked after by state Waqf Boards.
Land and Development Office (L&DO)
An office of the Union Housing Ministry that manages central government land in Delhi.

h: Student dies at Kasturba hostel in Siddipet, family alleges negligence
dek: A girl who fell ill after her first period got worse through the night and died by morning. Her family now wants an inquiry.
body: A Class 10 student living in the hostel of Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya, Raghavapur, in Telangana's Siddipet district died on Thursday. According to the report, she had her first period at the hostel itself. The cause of death is not yet clear.

The girl had returned to the hostel on 24 October after spending the Dussehra holidays at home. According to Navata, SHO of Siddipet Rural police station, she had not told anyone about her period. On Wednesday morning hostel staff informed her parents about her condition and asked them to take her home. The family said they were tied up with work and would come the next morning.

At night her condition got worse. A teacher called the family again to ask whether she should be taken to hospital. She was admitted to a government hospital, but died by morning. That is, from the time the family was informed on Wednesday morning until her condition worsened at night, the sick child stayed in the hostel, and the decision to take her to hospital was stuck waiting for the family's word.

On Thursday the family and local leaders sat in protest outside the mortuary of Siddipet Government Hospital, demanding an inquiry. BRS MLA Kotha Prabhakar Reddy accused the hostel of negligence and demanded 20 lakh rupees in compensation for the family. Police have registered a case of suspicious death under Section 194 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita.
nazar: Kasturba Gandhi schools are built especially for girls from poor, Dalit, Adivasi and backward families, whose parents are often daily wage earners who cannot take even a day off. So the hostel bears the first responsibility for a child's health, not sending her home. The real cause of death will be settled by the inquiry, but the question must be asked now: why did a whole night pass before the sick child was taken to hospital, and why do these hostels have no nurse or counsellor to talk about periods?
sawal: Who bears the first responsibility for a sick child in a hostel?
ref: Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya
Residential schools run under a central scheme that give girls from deprived sections schooling from Class 6 upwards and a place to live.
Section 194 BNSS
The section that replaced Section 174 of the old CrPC, under which police investigate unnatural or suspicious deaths.

h: Village choking on smoke can protest at the cremation ground: Madras High Court
dek: Police had stopped a protest by a Mayiladuthurai village battling pollution from a government rice mill; the High Court said the right to protest cannot be crushed at the very start.
body: The Madras High Court has allowed the people of Sitharkadu village in Tamil Nadu's Mayiladuthurai district to hold a protest at the cremation ground. In M. Anburaj v. District Collector, Justice V. Lakshminarayanan said the right to protest cannot be suppressed at its very start. Police had refused permission just a few hours before the protest due on 2 August, and a village resident had filed a petition against this.

The villagers allege that a rice mill of the Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation causes heavy air pollution and the air around it has turned bad. They have been raising their voice against it since 2006. They also appealed to the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board, but according to the petition, the effluent treatment plant near the mill does not work at all. When nothing came of the other constitutional routes, people planned to sit in protest at the cremation ground.

The court said protest is a form of expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. The judge also held that by drawing officials' attention to pollution, the villagers are fulfilling their fundamental duties under Article 51A, which include protecting the environment. Withholding permission on the basis of a vague fear alone is not justified.

The High Court set aside the police refusal and allowed the protest at the cremation ground from 29 November. The condition is that the protest stays peaceful and the organisers give the police a list of participants in advance.
nazar: That a village which has put up with a government mill's smoke for twenty years had to go to court just to sit and protest peacefully says a lot on its own. When the polluter is itself a government corporation, farmers, workers and villagers are left only with peaceful protest. The point that a protest cannot be stopped on a vague fear is a useful precedent against restrictions imposed across the country, though conditions like demanding a list of participants also jar.
sawal: Why did the village have to choose a cremation ground to be heard on pollution?
ref: Article 19(1)(a)
The provision giving every citizen freedom of speech and expression. Courts treat peaceful protest as part of it.
Article 51A(g)
The fundamental duty of citizens to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, rivers, lakes and wildlife.

h: In potters' homes before Diwali: clay costs more, diyas sell for less
dek: Prajapati families in Sultanpur village, Varanasi, have been making diyas for months, but rising costs and falling demand have dimmed their biggest earning season.
body: Sultanpur village in the Chiraigaon block of Varanasi district. For about ten Prajapati families here, the run-up to Diwali is the most important earning chance of the year. Two months ahead, the work of kneading clay, shaping diyas (clay lamps), drying and firing them begins, and the elderly, women and children all lend a hand.

This time the worry is cost. Poonam from one family says clay that once came for a thousand or fifteen hundred rupees has now reached four thousand, and good clay is hard to find. Cow-dung cakes for the kiln and paint for decoration have also become dearer. Abhishek Kumar Prajapati reckons that a hundred rupees of paint barely covers a hundred and fifty diyas, while buyers want cheap diyas and often even the labour does not pay off. If it rains the kiln will not light, and there is no space to store finished goods.

Falling demand is the second blow. According to Meena, homes that once lit a hundred diyas now make do with twenty-five. Pots and other traditional vessels sell less, and plastic has replaced children's clay toys. Competing with machine-made decorative diyas is not easy either.

Amarjeet Prajapati, who has done this work for thirty years, recalls that his family once sold eight to ten thousand diyas in a single Diwali; now the whole neighbourhood's sales have shrunk to between two and five thousand. The women of the house go to cook and wash dishes in other homes. The educated sons did not find jobs to match their studies; one drives an auto, the other does daily labour. Five families live in one government house.

The report's question is how long a skill that cannot run a household will survive. The new generation is turning away from this work, yet the wheel is still turning in these homes, on the small hope that the diyas will sell and some wage will be left after costs.
nazar: The hands behind the light of Diwali mostly belong to backward and artisan castes, and the market has slowly pushed them to the margins. Slogans like 'vocal for local' will stay hollow until some policy reaches the ground on basics like access to clay, cheap fuel, storage space and a fair price.

The most painful thing in this story is that the sense of the work being 'lowly' is also driving young people away from it. This tradition will survive only if both respect for the skill and the earnings return.
sawal: How many diyas did you buy from a potter this Diwali?
ref: Prajapati community
The common name in north India for the Kumhar (potter) community that makes clay pots. In most states it is counted among the Other Backward Classes.
Khabar Lahariya
An organisation of rural women journalists that began in Bundelkhand and reports from villages in Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar.

h: Thailand: seven years of lawsuits against those who stood with workers
dek: An appeals court will rule on 2 November in a defamation case by the poultry firm Thammakaset, and the rights group Fortify Rights has demanded that the case be thrown out.
body: Since 2016, the Thai poultry company Thammakaset has been known for the lawsuits it has slapped on its critics. It began when migrant workers from Myanmar on its farm complained of exploitation. According to a statement by Fortify Rights published on Prachatai English, the company has since filed at least 37 complaints against 22 human rights defenders, most of them women, and in most cases the courts ruled against the company.

The latest case involves three women: senator and former national human rights commissioner Angkhana Neelapaijit, Fortify Rights director Puttanee Kangkun, and former staff member Thanaporn Saleephol. They face 30 charges of criminal defamation over 30 social media posts. The posts expressed solidarity with activists facing lawsuits. Each charge carries up to two years in prison and a fine of two lakh (200,000) baht.

The lower court acquitted all three in August 2023, yet the case is still on appeal, and the verdict is due on 2 November 2026. The group's senior director Peter Bouckaert called it an abuse of the judicial process and said the government should decriminalise defamation.

The statement recalls that in May 2026 the President of the Thai Supreme Court issued recommendations to dismiss criminal cases filed in bad faith at the very start, but they do not apply at the appeal stage. According to the group, such lawsuits also go against Thailand's action plan on business and human rights, in which protecting defenders is a basic pillar.
nazar: This case shows that the fight for workers' rights does not stay inside the factory or farm; those who speak up for them are also dragged into court. In India too, Adivasis, farmers and journalists who raise their voices against mining, dams and industries are tied up for years in defamation and other cases.
A law that treats defamation as a crime becomes a tool of intimidation in the hands of the powerful. The demand to make it a civil matter is as necessary here as in Thailand.
sawal: Whom does the fear of jail for criticism protect?
ref: SLAPP
Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation: lawsuits whose aim is less to win and more to silence critics by tying them up in cost and fear.
Fortify Rights
An independent human rights group working in Southeast Asia that investigates and advocates on cases of migrant workers, refugees and activists.
photo_note: Representative image: women gleaning leftover ears of grain in a field, Jean-François Millet; not a picture of the Baiga community.

h: The hero officer show: when just doing your duty becomes news
dek: On Hindwi's Bela, Shashank Mishra writes an open letter to Maharashtra officer Tukaram Mundhe, asking why we turn inspections and raids into such a celebration.
body: In the Bela section of Hindwi, Shashank Mishra has written a letter addressed to Tukaram Mundhe. According to the writer, Mundhe is in the headlines these days for inspections of and notices to companies at Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration. The letter opens with the film 'Nayak' (Hero), in which a chief minister for a day catches cheating with the scales at a ration shop and the crowd claps.

The writer has no complaint about Mundhe's zeal. His worry is that we have come to treat inspection as an extraordinary event. A road gets built when an officer is due to visit, a hospital's broken water cooler shows up on the day of the tour, the mid-day meal improves that very day. Despite so many inspections, adulterated ghee, paneer without milk and fake bottled water are sold openly in the market.

The letter says seizures, bulldozers and sealing have now become a kind of fantasy. People watch someone's house being pulled down and take it for justice, and the question of process or outcome is left behind. As examples, the writer recalls the Aryan Khan drugs case and the media trial after Sushant Singh Rajput's death.

The writer also points to double standards: an anti-encroachment drive looks good until your own balcony is broken. Citing the films 'Gulaal' and 'Newton', he says that worshipping an honest officer is itself a statement of the system's failure.

In the end the letter's test is clear: the success of democracy should be measured not by the number of notices and demolished homes, but by how rarely such actions are needed. The writer hopes for the day when an officer doing his job is no longer news at all.
nazar: This letter catches a great sickness of our times: spectacle in place of justice. The celebration of the bulldozer weighs heaviest on the settlements where the poor, Muslims, Dalits and street vendors live. Real protection from adulteration comes from daily oversight, accountable institutions and the rights of workers and consumers, not from a single hero.
sawal: Do we want justice, or the spectacle of justice?
ref: Tukaram Mundhe
An IAS officer of the Maharashtra cadre, known for tough action and frequent transfers. According to the writer, he is in the news these days for Food and Drug Administration inspections.
Bela
Hindwi's prose section, where essays, letters, memoirs and commentary are published.

h: Cinema's comrade: why the leftist hero matters even more today
dek: On Hindwi, Dinesh Shrinet explores the tradition of workers, movements and Lal Salaam (red salute) in Telugu, Malayalam, Bengali and Hindi films.
body: In Hindwi's 'Unframed' column, Dinesh Shrinet looks at how popular Indian cinema has put left politics, trade unions and movements on screen. His opening argument is that in a time of right-wing rise, when 'leftist' has become an insult for some, such films matter even more.

From Telugu cinema he picks three films. In 'Dear Comrade', left politics is mostly a backdrop for romance, yet the idea of resistance comes through a simple story. The hero of 'Shyam Singha Roy' is an atheist activist who stands up against the devadasi system and caste. 'Virata Parvam' is a tragedy of love amid the Naxal movement, but the writer complains that it shows the movement not as an idea but as a package of guns, uniforms and jungle.

This strand is strongest in Malayalam cinema, and the writer credits Kerala's communist politics and union movement for it. The line runs from 1970's 'Ningalenne Communistakki' (You Made Me a Communist) to 2017's 'Sakhavu' (Comrade), which has a leader organising tea plantation workers.

In Hindi, the worker's question kept coming up, from Khwaja Ahmad Abbas's 'Dharti Ke Lal' (Children of the Earth) and Chetan Anand's 'Neecha Nagar' (Lowly City) to 'Naya Daur', 'Namak Haraam' and 'Coolie'. The writer treats Govind Nihalani's 'Aakrosh' and 'Ardh Satya' and Mrinal Sen's Calcutta trilogy as the yardstick for films that shake the mind more than the heart.
In conclusion Shrinet says that compared with the urban, lonely hero of the last decade and a half, a hero who is leftist or atheist and stands with the oppressed is brave and necessary.
nazar: When most heroes on screen are either nationalist warriors or lone successful men, this article reminds us that our cinema also has a long tradition of the struggles of workers, farmers, Dalits and Adivasis. Treating equality and opposition to religious bigotry as heroism is a cultural answer to today's politics.
sawal: Why doesn't today's Hindi cinema make a worker its hero?
ref: Neecha Nagar
Chetan Anand's 1946 film, a story of conflict between rich and poor neighbourhoods. The first Indian film to win the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival.
Mrinal Sen
A major Bengali filmmaker whose 'Calcutta 71', 'Padatik' and 'Chorus' are seen as a trilogy on the political turmoil of the seventies.

h: An owl on every branch: a satire on media, mafia and a stuck system
dek: On Sammukh, Shridhar Rao reviews Mukul Ranjan's novel, which looks inside the media industry through an attempt to launch a Bhojpuri channel.
body: On Sammukh, Shridhar Rao has written about Mukul Ranjan's novel 'Har Shaakh Par Ullu Baitha Hai' (An Owl Sits on Every Branch), published by Rajmangal Prakashan of Aligarh. Rao himself has worked for about twenty-five years at Doordarshan, Akashvani and several private channels, so he knows the media world from the inside.

According to the reviewer, it is a sharp, philosophical satire on a system where everyone looks busy, meetings, files and plans keep going, but real change never comes. The story opens with an attempt to launch a Bhojpuri channel called 'Birha', for a few pages starts to feel like a crime thriller with bullets and mystery, and then becomes an inside picture of the media industry.

Rao praises the characters most, especially Iltija. Every character has their own speech: a mix of Hindi and English, Bhojpuri, Maithili and the language of the underworld. In the kidnapping section the kidnappers call Iltija 'didi' (elder sister), which the reviewer sees as a study of the tangled relationship between crime and morality, and also raises the question of why many white-collar people are lower than these criminals.

The novel's range goes beyond the media to politics, the mafia, black money, foreign financial webs and corporate greed. The scene with vastu consultants in the channel's office is a jab at the thinking that looks for solutions to real problems in charms and superstition. Because of the writer's TV and film experience, the story moves scene by scene like a screenplay.

The reviewer also notes one flaw: a character named Karnam Saraswati suddenly disappears from the story. Still, his verdict is that this novel, full of mystery, humour and satire, will especially appeal to young readers.
nazar: There is little fiction in Hindi about the media, even though TV channels today set the terms of democracy's debate. If this novel shows how the nexus of crime, political patronage and money works behind the glitter, it helps turn the reader from a consumer of news into a citizen who asks questions.
sawal: When everyone looks busy and nothing changes, who is accountable?
ref: Har shaakh pe ullu baitha hai
Part of a famous couplet meaning that when useless people sit everywhere, the garden can only come to a bad end. A common idiom for mocking a system in ruin.
Sammukh
A Hindi literary web magazine that publishes poetry, stories, criticism, translations and reviews.

h: The Talat Aziz film that was never released
dek: The new instalment of Anirudh Sharma's column 'Ilmi-Filmi' on Sammukh tells the story of a ghazal singer's unfinished film dream and Mehdi Hassan's only Hindi film song.
body: Filmmaker Anirudh Sharma, author of 'Cinema Saptak', writes a column called 'Ilmi-Filmi' on Sammukh. This time the piece is on 'Dhun', and on ghazal singer Talat Aziz, who had made his own mark in ghazal singing in the eighties and whose presence made people advise him to go into films.

According to the writer, Mahesh Bhatt heard Talat live and used his songs in his 1989 film 'Daddy'. After this, a film was planned with Talat in the lead, produced by his wife Beena Aziz. The music was by Laxmikant-Pyarelal, and HMV released its cassette in 1991. In the film Talat played a jazz singer who comes from a small town and becomes a star.

The most interesting thing in the piece is a song the writer describes as Mehdi Hassan's first and only Hindi film song. Mehdi Hassan and Talat sang it together. Talat considered him his ustad (master), and the song was made at his wish, though the composer duo was at first not fully sure about the decision.

Then comes the incompleteness. According to the writer, the film was finished and got its censor certificate in 1996, but it has not been released to this day. The reason is recorded nowhere, and Talat himself ends the matter by saying only 'for some reasons'. The writer wonders how many dreams Talat must have seen and lost over these years.

The piece also has the writer's own memory: a fast song from this album playing at a wedding in 1991, when he was a child. He still listens to this album and asks readers whether they have heard these songs.
nazar: There is no count of how many finished films lie locked in cans in our film industry, and the labour of artists is buried with them. A song shared by Mehdi Hassan from across the border and Talat Aziz from this side reminds us that the heritage of music does not recognise the line of Partition.
sawal: Whose responsibility is the legacy of films locked in cans?
ref: Mehdi Hassan
Pakistan's great ghazal singer (1927-2012), called 'Shahenshah-e-Ghazal' (king of ghazal). He was born in Luna village in Rajasthan.
Talat Aziz
A ghazal singer born in Hyderabad who also sang in films such as 'Umrao Jaan' and 'Bazaar'.

h: Reels on the metro: dance, hate and astrology in a single swipe
dek: Rachit's satirical column 'Reel Rasacharya' on Hindwi reads the mood of a whole society from a stranger's reel feed on one Delhi Metro ride.
body: In Hindwi's Bela section, Rachit writes a satirical series called 'Reel Rasacharya' (master of reel flavours). In this instalment he is on the Delhi Metro, where the station announcement and the sound of a reel from someone's phone blend together, and he cannot tell which side the doors will open.

A little earlier the metro had announced that making reels is not allowed. The writer jokes that nobody minds abuse and shoving here, but if a girl dances, culture is in crisis. A song from the nineties, which once played worn thin on cassettes, has come back riding the algorithm.

The feed of a man standing nearby is reflected in the window glass, so everyone sitting opposite can watch it. In turn it shows dancing women, a clip about danger to nationalism and religion, some old singer and an astrology reel. To the writer it seems a sample of the country's mixed mood: no reel connects to the last, yet they all strike one note, and the viewer smiles, gets angry, believes and forgets.

In this crowd one man is reading a book, and he looks the strangest. The writer says that in this coach the book is a minority, and minorities often seem strange. People used to miss their stations because they dozed off; now it is because of reels.
In the end the writer has to get off at Mayur Vihar and still does not know which way the door will open. That question is the essence of the whole piece: is any clear message left in this noise?
nazar: This light piece says something serious: hate clips are now served without a pause between dance and astrology, and in that ease they become normal. The climate against minorities is often built from feeds like this, and even a small resistance like a book matters to guard your own gaze.
sawal: What is your feed turning you into?
ref: Reel
Short videos on Instagram and other platforms, shown one after another without end by an algorithm.
